item.title: Westside Gunn Sets December Drop For Saucony Sneakers Honoring Big Dump
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Westside Gunn gives his Big Dump tribute a December release date and tells WrestleCade attendees how to ask about early pairs.
item.content:encoded:
Westside Gunn is putting the name of his late friend Big Dump on a Saucony sneaker due December 4.

The Buffalo rapper showed the Grid Jazz 9 in an Instagram post on Thanksgiving Eve and called the design both “Big Dumps” and “Heelmatics.”

“I WISH MY BRO DUMP WAS HERE TO WEAR THESE,” Westside Gunn wrote alongside the preview.

He invited people headed to WrestleCade on Friday to ask about getting a pair early and indicated he might let some pairs go on Black Friday.

Big Dump, also known as Infinite, was the friend Gunn mourned after his death in 2024.

Gunn dedicated part of that year’s five-track 11 EP to him, putting his name on “Big Dump Ballad” and his image on the cover.

Gunn showed Fat Joe and Jadakiss a pre-production sample on Joe and Jada before sharing the release date.

“I got his name on the back of the shoe,” Gunn said, pointing out the tribute to Big Dump. He said the sample wasn’t for sale and showed the hosts where he’d replaced a logo with a scorpion.

The sample follows a separate “Awesome God” edition that Saucony released in August. That shoe used the same Grid Jazz 9 shape and drew on Gunn’s Flygod Is An Awesome God series.

The company said he recorded portions of the trilogy’s third installment at its Boston innovation hub.

The possibility of an early pair came up as he promoted his 4th Rope wrestling show in North Carolina.

The promotion’s Heels Have Eyes event is scheduled for 9:30 P.M. Friday at the Benton Convention Center in Winston-Salem, North Carolina. The Hardys and Real1 are among the wrestlers advertised for the show.

Gunn’s Friday plans also include a separate Machinegun Black Friday clothing and art drop, which he previewed in another Instagram post.

He said that release would go online at noon Eastern and that the one-of-a-kind pieces would be offered at WrestleCade.

The sneaker’s other nickname echoes the title of Heelmatic, the album Gunn released this month through Griselda and Mass Appeal.

item.title: MO3’s Brother Co Gotti Held Without Bond In Texas Firearm Case
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Co Gotti remains in a Texas jail after a judge denies bond in an existing firearm case tied to a September indictment.
item.content:encoded:
Co Gotti is in a Texas jail after a judge took away his bond in a firearm case that dates back to September.

The Dallas rapper and younger brother of MO3 was booked into the Collin County jail on November 20, two days after the court ordered him held without bond.

The court docket shows prosecutors moved on November 18 to revoke bond and keep Co Gotti in custody pending trial.

“Court orders bond held insufficient. Defendant to be held without bond,” the entry reads.

A grand jury indicted him on September 29 for unlawful possession of a firearm by a felon over an alleged July 26 offense. The docket lists an October 23 first appearance and shows the firearm case as pending, with no judgment listed.

The jail’s booking record also lists warrants issued November 18 after bonds were found insufficient in two other cases.

One is a second firearm-possession case filed in November 2025 over an alleged June 13, 2025 offense. The other is a charge of evading arrest or detention with a vehicle filed in February over an alleged October 2025 offense.

The same booking record lists bonds forfeited in two misdemeanor cases.

The marijuana case was filed in August 2025 and involves alleged possession of less than two ounces, while the separate evading-arrest case was filed October 28 over an alleged incident in February.

The docket in the latter case records that his name was called three times at the courtroom door on November 20 and went unanswered before the bond was forfeited.

In a separate case, a Dallas County jury convicted Yella Beezy of capital murder on November 11, six years to the day after MO3 was killed, and he was sentenced to life in prison without parole before his lawyer reportedly filed a notice of appeal on November 20.

item.title: Don Cornelius’ Son Is Writing A Book About The Man Who Built Soul Train
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Don Cornelius' son Tony is working on a book about the Soul Train creator as the awards return to Chicago on television.
item.content:encoded:
Don Cornelius built a nationally syndicated show with help from his family, and now his son is writing about his life.

Tony Cornelius told WGN-TV he’s working on a book about his father and what he left behind, as the awards carrying the Soul Train name prepare to air after a taping in the city where the program began.

Tony remembers that putting Soul Train on television was a family job before there was a national audience. While his father worked to get the program off the ground, Tony recalled that “my mother was on the floor dealing with cue cards and signing up high schoolers to dance.”

Those teenagers joined a show that started on Chicago’s WCIU-TV on August 17, 1970, with Jerry Butler, the Emotions and the Chi-Lites on its first episode.

The Chi-Lites’ Marshall Thompson recalled that Chicago’s WVON was already playing the group’s records, but television gave them a chance to reach children coming home from school.

The Chicago program went into national syndication the following year, with production moving to Los Angeles and Afro Sheen founder George Johnson helping fund the expansion.

The dancers became as recognizable a part of the show as the singers, taking turns down the line that ran between two rows of their peers. Along with the dance line, the show had a scramble board on which dancers put letters in order to spell the name of a notable Black figure.

Tony eventually worked alongside his father as a producer, but his father made him start at the bottom and learn the work instead of handing him a senior job. Shemar Moore, who went on to host Soul Train, told AllHipHop that Don believed in him when he got the chance to take over the show.

Tony went on to launch the Soul Train Cruise in 2013, bringing artists from the show’s era back together for live performances.

Tony is also an executive producer of the 2026 ceremony, which was taped November 5 at Chicago’s Harris Theater in Millennium Park. Anthony Anderson hosted the return of the Soul Train Awards, the first edition since 2023.

The ceremony airs Friday, November 27, on BET and CBS at 8 P.M. Eastern.

item.title: Tank Recalls BMF Putting Money Into The Album That Revived His Career
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Tank recalls Black Mafia Family putting money into his comeback album before his own label heard it and stepped back in.
item.content:encoded:
Tank says Black Mafia Family invested in the music that brought him back after his career stalled.

He told the TFU Podcast that after Blackground Records heard the songs that became Sex, Love & Pain, it objected to BMF moving ahead with the project because Tank was still signed to the label.

Tank traced the offer of help to a man he knew who had spent time in prison with people willing to back a project. The singer said he hadn’t heard of BMF when the introduction came up in the early 2000s.

“And they flew us down to Miami,” Tank said, recalling that he took his girlfriend, Zena, who is now his wife.

Tank remembered a line of luxury cars and a room where he thought people were walking off with bottles.

He said he later learned the group had paid for the whole club. What began as an introduction in Miami, he recalled, helped get him back in the business.

BMF co-founder Big Meech had his own music operation, describing himself to AllHipHop as the head of BMF’s record label.

Tank said BMF spent money on Sex, Love & Pain while he was still under contract with Blackground.

He recalled how people at the label reacted: “When they heard the music, they was like, ‘No, that’s our artist. You can’t do that.'”

The music also marked a new stretch of studio work with The Underdogs, whose approach Tank credited with improving his craft.

He singled out Damon Thomas and Harvey Mason Jr. when he explained what he learned from the team. Thomas also had ties to BMF co-founder Terry “Southwest T” Flenory: AllHipHop reported in 2007 that Thomas was called to testify in the federal BMF case after police seized about $5 million in jewelry from Flenory during a 2005 traffic stop. Thomas denied the jewelry belonged to him.

Blackground released the album in May 2007, and it peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard 200 and No. 1 on the Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart. It was Tank’s first album in five years.

The Recording Academy later nominated Sex, Love & Pain for Best R&B Album and “Please Don’t Go” for Best Male R&B Vocal Performance.

item.title: Chris Rock Puts Druski’s SNL Confidence In Eddie Murphy’s Company
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Chris Rock puts Druski in rare company after his Saturday Night Live debut and explains what stood out to him onstage.
item.content:encoded:
Chris Rock reached back to his own comedy hero to explain what he saw in Druski’s first night hosting Saturday Night Live.

In an interview with Ben Stiller on The A24 Podcast, Rock said he rarely sees a young comedian that composed on live television, especially in a role that asks its host to switch characters all night.

Rock had Eddie Murphy in mind when he tried to put Druski’s performance in perspective.

Rock called Druski “the most confident, well-adjusted, young comedian I’ve ever seen” and added, “It was so healthy.” “The only guy that I’ve ever seen that confident was Eddie Murphy,” Rock said.

He brought up Druski’s Joe Jackson spoof in the same exchange and wanted to pull it up for Stiller while they discussed how comics find an audience now. Rock also praised the show itself, not just Druski’s delivery.

Rock’s comparison carries some history for the comedian who made it. Earlier in the conversation, Rock and Stiller laughed about how Murphy was only about four years older than either of them but seemed to belong to an older generation when they were coming up.

Rock said he still felt some of that awe decades later and recalled going to Murphy’s house to watch a Michael Jackson movie together.

Rock was in Studio 8H for the November 7 show, and he appeared during the closing goodnights alongside Dave Chappelle, Michael B. Jordan and Austin Butler.

Druski’s opening monologue included a visit from Emma Stone, his co-star in the baseball comedy The Catch, while The Strokes were the night’s musical guest. The episode drew 5.6 million television viewers, the show’s largest audience in two years.

Druski had been producing his own comedy online long before the NBC booking, including the mock auditions for his fictional label Coulda Been Records.

Stiller wondered whether that kind of head start changed how younger comedians handled a national stage because they had already built an audience on their own.

Rock agreed that younger comics often seem more secure, though he said some bring that ease to stand-up without doing enough to make a joke land.

Druski’s next series, Collect & Praise, pairs him with Mike Epps and is part of a multiyear deal with Netflix.

item.title: Bobby Lytes Eyes Rehab And Gets Cardi B’s Support After Miami Club Incident
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Bobby Lytes considers treatment and apologizes to Deshae Frost as Cardi B tells him it's time to look out for himself.
item.content:encoded:
Bobby Lytes wants to look into rehab after a night out in Miami ended with a video of him getting stopped at a nightclub door.

The Love & Hip Hop: Miami cast member spoke about the encounter in a video on his Instagram, where he talked about Cardi B’s group arriving and spoke directly to streamer Deshae Frost.

Lytes said he’d come too far to let drugs cost him the life he’d built.

“I am going to look into going into some type of rehab,” Lytes said in the video. He asked viewers to hold him accountable without naming a program or giving a start date.

Cardi answered in the comments, opening with “I can’t wait” and telling Lytes she sees him as a good person. Cardi called him “a selfless person” before urging him to give himself the same care he gives other people.

“you always looking out for others is time for you to look out for yourself…WE ROOTING FOR YOU !!!!” Cardi wrote.

Lytes replied that he loved her and thanked her for the encouragement.

Lytes’ apology to Frost came with an acknowledgment that the two don’t know each other personally.

Lytes said he’d been joking but still owed Frost a public apology, and he separately apologized to the people who work with Cardi. He opened his video by saying he hadn’t recorded it to excuse how he acted.

Lytes also gave his own account of the night Cardi’s group went to E11EVEN Miami. He said a separate situation had happened in the same spot outside the club about an hour before Cardi got there.

According to Lytes, she didn’t know security would stop him, and he got through the door about three minutes later.

The clip from November 21 showed Lytes trying to get the rapper’s attention while her group went inside.

Cardi had already denied telling security to keep him out and said members of her team helped get him in, including stylist Tokyo Stylez. In 2021, when a group of Black women said they’d been turned away at E11EVEN, Cardi asked security to let them in, and Lytes later spoke out against the club.

item.title: Crime Mob’s “Knuck If You Buck” Could Become Georgia’s Official State Song
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: OutKast, Crime Mob and Usher are among nine choices for a second Georgia state song, alongside "Georgia on My Mind."
item.content:encoded:
OutKast and Crime Mob have songs on Georgia’s shortlist for a new state anthem alongside the Ray Charles classic that’s already on the books.

State Rep. Eric Bell, a Jonesboro Democrat, is asking residents to weigh in before he introduces legislation to give a second song an official designation.

OutKast’s “Hey Ya!” and Crime Mob’s “Knuck If You Buck” make up only part of the Hip-Hop and R&B contingent on the nine-song list Bell’s office released.

Field Mob’s “Georgia” features Ludacris and Jamie Foxx, while Usher’s “Yeah!” pairs him with Lil Jon and Ludacris. F.L.Y.’s “Swag Surfin'” is on the list, too.

The rap records share a ballot with Alan Jackson’s “Chattahoochee,” the Zac Brown Band’s “Chicken Fried,” Lauren Alaina’s “Georgia Peaches” and Sugarland’s “Something More.”

“Now, we’re inviting Georgians to help decide which song best represents the Georgia of today,” Bell said in the announcement. The survey also lets residents write in a song rather than choose from the nine nominees.

Bell says the new category wouldn’t touch “Georgia on My Mind,” which the state adopted in 1979.

Hoagy Carmichael and Stuart Gorrell wrote that song, and Ray Charles made it famous and sang it for lawmakers when the measure passed. Bell called his proposal “a totally different designation that will preserve the past while representing a future that people can relate to” in an interview with CBS News Atlanta.

Bell said he hasn’t introduced a bill and expects to keep the survey open through most of the upcoming legislative session.

A favorite in the poll wouldn’t become official on the strength of those votes alone: A proposal would still go to committees and need votes in the Georgia House and Senate.

OutKast’s pick comes from Speakerboxxx/The Love Below, and it reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100.

Janelle Monáe performed “Hey Ya!” when OutKast entered the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2025, with Big Boi performing elsewhere in the tribute alongside Sleepy Brown.

Bell told CBS News Atlanta he has a favorite but hasn’t named it publicly because he doesn’t want to steer the vote.

item.title: Belly Gang Kushington Says Wale Washed Him On Summer Walker Collab “Bonnet”
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Belly Gang Kushington remembers hearing Wale's verse on "Bonnet" and explains how a Kirk Franklin remix came together.
item.content:encoded:
Belly Gang Kushington knows who won the matchup on his song with Wale.

The Atlanta rapper singled out “Bonnet,” his track with Wale and Summer Walker, when Incognito asked about his collaborators in an interview on K97.5’s Posted on the Corner.

Belly Gang Kushington said his team sent the track over and waited to hear what Wale would do with it.

“We sent it to him. He blew it out the water,” the rapper told Incognito. “When I heard it, I’m like, oh yeah, I lost on this song.”

Belly Gang Kushington also described changing the way he’d built songs since his first album, when he came into sessions with a plan already drawn up.

For Good Dope Sell Itself, he took his cues from the production instead of trying to make it fit a song he’d already mapped out. He said he can tell within about a second whether a beat has enough to hold his attention.

The decision to send “Bonnet” to Wale was one way a collaboration came together, but Belly Gang Kushington said the idea for a Kirk Franklin remix came from both directions.

He said his team and Franklin’s reached out at the same time. The rapper also recalled getting lemon pepper wings with Franklin in Miami after they connected.

Franklin first released “This Time” with GloRilla, and the remix isn’t part of Good Dope Sell Itself.

The album is Belly Gang Kushington’s second, following the 2025 release The Streets Is Yours. The 12-track project, released November 13 on LVRN Records, features 21 Savage on “WTF GOIN,” YKNIECE on “Doctor Mama,” and YFN Lucci on “Show Me Sum.”

Belly Gang Kushington named his tour after the 21 Savage collaboration and booked the opening night at the Tabernacle in Atlanta on November 25. He’d already played “WTF GOIN” alongside 21 Savage during Usher and Chris Brown’s tour, and he told the radio audience to arrive early for his hometown headlining date.

The WTF GOIN Tour heads to the Shelter in Detroit on December 3 before a December 8 date at House of Blues in Houston.

item.title: Ashanti Explains Why She’s Waiting To Have Another Baby With Nelly
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Ashanti wants another baby with Nelly, but she's figuring out how to make time for a newborn while their careers keep moving.
item.content:encoded:
Ashanti is looking at the calendar before she and Nelly try to give their son a sibling.

The two are already parents to their son KK, and the question of whether to grow their family comes up in the second season of their Peacock series.

For Ashanti, the decision comes down to how much of her time she’d want to give a newborn.

“I have to give my undivided attention,” she said in an interview with People. “When I have a child, everything kind of stops.”

That pause is hard to picture with both artists making plans for the coming year. Ashanti is working on new music, and the couple is planning to tour together in 2027.

She’s been looking for a stretch when she could slow down, but Nelly laughed at the idea that they could pin down the timing that neatly: “She’s finding out that life just happens.”

The couple already has a system for making their schedules work as parents. They use a shared calendar and have agreed not to be apart for more than 30 days.

When Ashanti gets a few days off between commitments, she looks for a chance to take KK to wherever Nelly is working.

The pair expects KK to come on the joint tour and spend time on both parents’ buses. Ashanti said he already comes along to her shows more often than he travels with his dad. On flights, she said, he greets the people around him and settles in with Bluey.

The couple’s experience raising KK is part of what viewers see in Nelly & Ashanti: We Belong Together, which returned to Peacock on November 19 with eight episodes.

The new season also follows them as they decide whether to show him on social media and talk about where the family might settle once he’s ready to start school. New York, where Ashanti grew up, and Nelly’s hometown of St. Louis are both in the conversation.

Ashanti and Nelly first met at the 2003 Grammy Awards, reunited about two decades later and welcomed KK in July 2024 after marrying the previous year.

item.title: Tennessee Museum Extends Rap Contest Built On Zora Neale Hurston’s Recordings
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: ETSU's Reece Museum extended its rap contest to January 18, giving artists more time to build songs from 1930s recordings.
item.content:encoded:
Zora Neale Hurston helped record folk songs on a Georgia island in 1935, and a Tennessee museum is giving rappers more time to turn those recordings into new songs. East Tennessee State University’s Reece Museum extended the entry deadline for From the Archives to the Mic to Monday, January 18, 2027.

Three of the four tracks contestants can build on come from that Georgia field trip. Hurston, Alan Lomax and Mary Elizabeth Barnicle recorded at Frederica on St. Simons Island, where John Davis and his group sang the material used on “Down Bad.” “Favored” and “Ring a Ding” draw on performances by girls whose names aren’t listed in the archive.

Barnicle also recorded the church congregation behind the fourth track. She traveled to Pineville, Kentucky, in 1938, and that recording became the basis for “Cinema.” The Georgia trip had captured more than songs: Its recordings include church services, children’s games and interviews with Gullah speakers.

Those older recordings reached the contest through Future Proof, a project that producer Nathan Blye and performer Josh Outsey brought to the museum’s Hip Hop Listening Room. Blye and his team spent eight months going through thousands of recordings as they worked on the project. “Hip-Hop is taking scraps and making them shine,” Blye told the East Tennessean.

Entrants now have to do that work with one of the four approved tracks, making it a central part of an original song.

The museum asks for the recording, written lyrics and a 100- to 200-word statement explaining how the archival material shaped the entry.

It recommends songs of two to five minutes and bars any extra samples the artist doesn’t have permission to use.

Judges give originality the most weight, with use of the sample and the quality of the lyrics and songwriting tied behind it.

They also score how well the artist connects the song to the people or places heard in the original recording. The prize announced so far is a $100 gift certificate from Laced Up Cuts and Kicks.

The museum plans to notify the winner by January 29 and put on a performance in February.
